content: The use of acupuncture as a treatment for stress urinary incontinence is becoming increasingly common, particularly in Asian regions. However, its clinical effectiveness and potential side effects have not been thoroughly evaluated. The objective of this study was to evaluate both the effectiveness and the side effects of acupuncture in managing stress urinary incontinence in adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Register (as of January 28, 2013), EMBASE, AMED, the Chinese Biomedical Literature Database (CBM), the Chinese Acupuncture Trials Register, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) (all searched as of February 20, 2013). Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed, and authors and trialists in the field were contacted for further information. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that investigated acupuncture as a standalone intervention for the treatment of stress urinary incontinence in adults. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, evaluated the quality of the trials, and extracted relevant data. Where appropriate, data were combined and analyzed using meta-analytic techniques. Out of 17 studies initially identified as potentially eligible, only one small trial involving 60 women met the inclusion criteria. This trial compared acupuncture to midodrine, a pharmacological agent used to treat hypotension. The trial was found to have a high risk of bias due to several methodological limitations, including the lack of concealment of randomization, absence of blinding in outcome assessment, and the inability to blind participants and healthcare providers to the interventions. Furthermore, the statistical methods employed in the trial were not adequately described. In this trial, a higher proportion of women in the acupuncture group showed improvement compared to the midodrine group (73% versus 33%; risk ratio [RR] 2.20, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.27 to 3.81). However, the cure rates between the two groups were low and not statistically significantly different (13% in the acupuncture group versus 7% in the midodrine group; RR 2.00, 95% CI 0.40 to 10.11). Adverse events were reported only in the midodrine group, with no adverse events noted in the acupuncture group. The authors concluded that the effectiveness of acupuncture for the treatment of stress urinary incontinence in adults remains uncertain. The evidence is insufficient to determine whether acupuncture is more effective than pharmacological treatment.
